title: Definition
body_md:
A $T_0$-quasi-metric space is \emph{$q$-plastic} if every bijective
nonexpansive self-map is an isometry. It is \emph{$q$-rigid} if every such map
is the identity. Thus $q$-rigidity implies $q$-plasticity; for symmetric $d$,
$q$-plasticity is metric plasticity.
head: environment

label: prop:totalbounded
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:totalbounded}
If $(X,d^s)$ is totally bounded, then $(X,d)$ is $q$-plastic.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Set $\rho(x,y)=d(x,y)+d(y,x)$. This is a metric with
$d^s\le\rho\le2d^s$, so it is totally bounded. A bijective
$d$-nonexpansive self-map $F$ is $\rho$-nonexpansive. Metric plasticity
\cite{Naimpally} yields
\[
d(Fx,Fy)+d(Fy,Fx)=d(x,y)+d(y,x).
\]
Each summand on the left is at most the corresponding summand on the right;
equality forces equality of both. This is the sum-metric mechanism used in
\cite{Zavarzina}, here formulated under $T_0$ separation.
head: environment

label: prop:dense
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:dense}
Suppose $(Y,d^s)$ is separable and every nonempty $d^s$-open subset
contains an uncountable $d^s$-compact subset. Then $Y$ contains a
$d^s$-dense $q$-rigid subspace.
head: environment
name: Metric dense-rigidity transfer

title: Proof
body_md:
The metric theorem of Banakh, Mazurenko and Zavarzina \cite{Banakh}
provides a dense subspace $A$ on which every bijective $d^s$-nonexpansive
self-map is the identity. Every $d$-nonexpansive map is also
$d^s$-nonexpansive, so $A$ is $q$-rigid.
head: environment

label: prop:contraction
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:contraction}
If a q-LCDH space $Y$ admits a bijective contraction, then every countable
dense subset $A\subseteq Y$ with at least two points admits a bijective
contraction and is not $q$-plastic. In particular, this holds for a countable
space whose bicompletion has those two properties.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $T$ have contraction constant $c$. It is continuous for $d^s$, and
surjectivity makes $T[A]$ dense: for $y=Tz$, approximate $z$ by points
of $A$. Choose $\varepsilon$ with $(1+\varepsilon)c<1$ and use q-LCDH
to obtain $g[T[A]]=A$. Then $g\circ T|_A$ is bijective and
\[
d(gTx,gTy)\le(1+\varepsilon)c\,d(x,y).
\]
The $T_0$ condition supplies a positive directed distance between two
distinct points, which this map strictly decreases. For the final assertion,
apply the argument to the canonical dense copy in the bicompletion.
head: environment

label: lem:relative
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $H(f)=g$. Nonexpansiveness and \eqref{eq:evaluation} give
$g_1(x)\le f_1(x)$ and $g_2(x)\le f_2(x)$ for every $x$.
The pair $g$ is ample, so minimality of $f$ gives $g=f$.
head: environment

label: lem:propagation
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The quasi-pseudometric $\delta(p,q)=D(Fp,Fq)$ is at most $D$ and agrees
with $D$ on the canonical copy. Tightness gives $\delta=D$.
head: environment

label: thm:inheritance
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:inheritance}
Suppose every bijective nonexpansive self-map of $Q(X)$ preserves $e(X)$
setwise. If $X$ is $q$-plastic, then $Q(X)$ is $q$-plastic. If $X$ is
$q$-rigid, then $Q(X)$ is $q$-rigid.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The restriction of a hull map induces a bijective nonexpansive self-map of
$X$. For $q$-plastic $X$, apply Lemma~\ref{lem:propagation}; for $q$-rigid
$X$, apply Lemma~\ref{lem:relative}.
head: environment

label: prop:upperline
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:upperline}
The space $(\mathbb R,u)$ is $q$-hyperconvex but not $q$-plastic.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For compatible double balls, the required inequalities are
$x_i-s_i\le w\le x_i+r_i$. Compatibility gives
$x_j-s_j\le x_i+r_i$ for all $i,j$, hence
\[
\sup_j(x_j-s_j)\le\inf_i(x_i+r_i).
\]
For a nonempty family, any fixed index $i_0$ bounds both quantities between
$x_{i_0}-s_{i_0}$ and $x_{i_0}+r_{i_0}$, so a real $w$ can be chosen
between them. The empty family has intersection $\mathbb R$.
Thus the space is $q$-hyperconvex. The bijection $T(t)=t/2$ satisfies
$u(Ts,Tt)=u(s,t)/2$, so it is nonexpansive and not an isometry.
head: environment

label: prop:linehull
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $t\in\mathbb R$ put $f_1^t(x)=(x-t)^+$ and $f_2^t(x)=(t-x)^+$ on $A$.
Ampleness follows from $(y-x)^+\le(t-x)^++(y-t)^+$.
Choosing points of $A$ below both $t,x$, and above both $t,x$, respectively,
verifies the two extremality identities \eqref{eq:extremal}, hence minimality.

Conversely, for a minimal pair $f$, set $t=\sup_{y\in A}(y-f_1(y))$.
Ampleness gives $y-f_1(y)\le x_0+f_2(x_0)$ for any fixed $x_0\in A$;
an individual term gives a finite lower bound. Thus $t\in\mathbb R$, and
\eqref{eq:extremal} gives
\[
f_2(x)=\sup_{y\in A}((y-x)^+-f_1(y))^+=(t-x)^+.
\]
Here the inner positive part equals $(y-x-f_1(y))^+$ because
$f_1(y)\ge0$. Substitution into the other identity gives
\[
f_1(x)=\sup_{y\in A}((x-y)^+-(t-y)^+)^+=(x-t)^+.
\]
The upper bound follows from the upper quasi-metric triangle inequality;
equality is attained using $y$ below both $x,t$. Thus every minimal pair
is $f^t$. The two suprema in \eqref{eq:hullmetric} both equal $(t-s)^+$
for $D(f^s,f^t)$, using points above both parameters for the first and
below both for the second. Finally, $e(a)=f^a$ for $a\in A$.
head: environment

label: prop:integers
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The symmetrization is the complete metric $|m-n|$. A bijective
$u$-nonexpansive $F$ is strictly increasing: for $m<n$,
$u(Fn,Fm)=0$ gives $Fm\le Fn$, and injectivity makes the inequality
strict. Surjectivity rules out gaps, so $F(n+1)=F(n)+1$.
Hence $F(n)=n+k$ for some integer $k$, and $F$ is an isometry.
Propositions~\ref{prop:linehull} and \ref{prop:upperline} identify the
hull as the non-$q$-plastic upper real line.
head: environment

label: cor:rigidfailure
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By \cite{Banakh}, there is a Euclidean-dense $A\subseteq\mathbb R$ whose
bijective Euclidean-nonexpansive self-maps are all the identity.
Every $u$-nonexpansive map is Euclidean-nonexpansive, so $(A,u)$ is
$q$-rigid. Density makes $A$ unbounded in both directions; apply
Proposition~\ref{prop:linehull}.
head: environment

label: prop:complements
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Proposition~\ref{prop:totalbounded}, a bijective nonexpansive hull map
is a $D$-isometry. It is therefore an order automorphism and preserves
$\bot,\top$, meets, joins and complemented elements. It preserves $e(X)$
setwise, so Theorem~\ref{thm:inheritance} gives $q$-rigidity.
head: environment

label: ex:rectangle
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:rectangle}
Let $a,b>0$, $a\ne b$, and set
\[
B=[0,a]\times[0,b],\qquad X=\{(0,0),(a,0),(0,b),(a,b)\}.
\]
Equip both spaces with $u_2(p,q)=\max\{(q_1-p_1)^+,(q_2-p_2)^+\}$.
We identify $Q(X)$ with $B$ and verify every hypothesis of
Proposition~\ref{prop:complements}. The rectangular hull geometry is known:
\cite[Example~2]{EndpointsII} identifies $B$ as the hull of its opposite
vertices $(a,0),(0,b)$; see also \cite{Willerton}. All four vertices are
used here so that the canonical copy equals the complemented elements.

\emph{Hull identification.} Write $L_1=a,L_2=b$. For a nonempty
compatible family $(z^\lambda,r_\lambda,s_\lambda)$ in $B$, the
double-ball conditions in coordinate $i$ are
$z_i^\lambda-s_\lambda\le w_i\le z_i^\lambda+r_\lambda$ and
$0\le w_i\le L_i$. Compatibility gives
\[
\max\{0,\sup_\mu(z_i^\mu-s_\mu)\}
\le \min\{L_i,\inf_\lambda(z_i^\lambda+r_\lambda)\}.
\]
The bounds are finite, since centres are in $[0,L_i]$ and a fixed index
bounds the suprema and infima. Choose each $w_i$ between them.
The empty family has intersection $B$, so $B$ is $q$-hyperconvex.

To check tightness over $X$, let $\delta\le u_2$ be a quasi-pseudometric
agreeing with $u_2$ on $X\times X$, and set
$c_1=(0,b),d_1=(a,0),c_2=(a,0),d_2=(0,b)$.
For $p,q\in B$,
$u_2(c_i,d_i)=L_i$, $u_2(c_i,p)=p_i$ and
$u_2(q,d_i)=L_i-q_i$. Therefore
\[
L_i=\delta(c_i,d_i)
\le\delta(c_i,p)+\delta(p,q)+\delta(q,d_i)
\le p_i+\delta(p,q)+L_i-q_i.
\]
Thus $\delta(p,q)\ge(q_i-p_i)^+$ in both coordinates, giving
$\delta=u_2$. The tight-envelope characterization \cite{Tight}
identifies $B$ with $Q(X)$ by an isometry carrying $e(X)$ to $X$.

\emph{Compactness.} The symmetrization of $u_2$ is the maximum norm metric.
The closed rectangle is compact in that metric.

\emph{Bounded lattice order.} The relation
$p\preceq q\iff u_2(q,p)=0$ is coordinatewise order. Its least and
greatest elements are $(0,0)$ and $(a,b)$; meets and joins are coordinatewise
minima and maxima. It is therefore a bounded lattice.

\emph{Complemented elements.} If $p,q$ are complements, then
$\min\{p_i,q_i\}=0$ and $\max\{p_i,q_i\}=L_i$.
Hence $p_i\in\{0,L_i\}$, so $p$ is a vertex. Conversely, the complement
of a vertex $p$ is $(a-p_1,b-p_2)$. Consequently $C(B)=X$, which gives
$C(Q(X))=e(X)$ under the hull identification.

\emph{Rigidity of the original space.} A bijective nonexpansive map of
the finite set $X$ has some power $F^N=\operatorname{id}$. The cyclic chain
\[
u_2(x,y)\ge u_2(Fx,Fy)\ge\cdots\ge u_2(F^Nx,F^Ny)=u_2(x,y)
\]
makes it an isometry and order automorphism. It fixes bottom and top.
The two remaining vertices are the atoms, whose distances from $(0,0)$
are $a$ and $b$. These are distinct, so the atoms are fixed as well.
Thus $X$ is $q$-rigid, and Proposition~\ref{prop:complements} makes $B$
$q$-rigid. For instance, take $a=1,b=2$.

If $a=b$, the three structural hypotheses still hold, but coordinate
transposition is a nonidentity isometry of both $X$ and $B$.
This verifies the separate role of $q$-rigidity of the original space.

name: A four-vertex asymmetric rectangle

label: def:interval
title: Definition
head: environment

label: prop:coordinates
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:coordinates}
Every two-sided directed interval satisfies
\[
d(x,y)=\max\{(d(a,y)-d(a,x))^+,(d(b,y)-d(b,x))^+\}.
\]
Thus $\Phi(x)=(d(a,x),d(b,x))$ is an isometric embedding into
$(\mathbb R^2,u_2)$ with bounded image, and
$d^s(x,y)=\|\Phi(x)-\Phi(y)\|_\infty$.
head: environment
name: Endpoint-coordinate representation

title: Proof
body_md:
The triangle inequality bounds each positive difference by $d(x,y)$.
If \eqref{eq:chainab} holds, then
\[
d(x,y)=d(a,b)-d(a,x)-d(y,b)\le d(a,y)-d(a,x),
\]
using $d(a,b)\le d(a,y)+d(y,b)$. If \eqref{eq:chainba} holds,
the same argument gives $d(x,y)\le d(b,y)-d(b,x)$.
This proves the formula. The $T_0$ condition makes $\Phi$ injective.
Every directed distance is at most $M=\max\{d(a,b),d(b,a)\}$ by
the chain condition, so $\Phi(I)\subseteq[0,M]^2$.
Taking the maximum for both orientations gives the metric identity.
head: environment

label: cor:intervalplastic
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:intervalplastic}
Every two-sided directed interval is $q$-plastic.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Its symmetrization is isometric to a bounded subset of the maximum norm
plane, hence is totally bounded. Apply Proposition~\ref{prop:totalbounded}.
head: environment

label: thm:endpoints
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:endpoints}
Let $(I,d)$ be a two-sided directed interval with endpoints $a,b$.
If $F:I\to(Y,\rho)$ is nonexpansive and preserves both directed endpoint
distances, then $F$ is an isometric embedding.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For an ordered pair satisfying \eqref{eq:chainab},
\begin{align*}
d(a,b)&=\rho(Fa,Fb)\\
&\le\rho(Fa,Fx)+\rho(Fx,Fy)+\rho(Fy,Fb)\\
&\le d(a,x)+d(x,y)+d(y,b)=d(a,b).
\end{align*}
Equality throughout forces $\rho(Fx,Fy)=d(x,y)$.
For \eqref{eq:chainba}, use the chain starting at $b$ and ending at $a$
and preservation of $d(b,a)$. Thus every directed distance is preserved.
head: environment

label: thm:diameter
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The interval is bounded by Proposition~\ref{prop:coordinates}.
Let $\Delta=\operatorname{diam}_d(I)=d(a,b)$ and let $F$ be bijective and nonexpansive.
Choose $x,y$ with $Fx=a,Fy=b$. Then
$\Delta=d(Fx,Fy)\le d(x,y)\le\Delta$.
Uniqueness gives $x=a,y=b$, so $F$ fixes the endpoints.
Theorem~\ref{thm:endpoints} makes $F$ an isometry, which preserves
$\Phi$. Injectivity of $\Phi$ in Proposition~\ref{prop:coordinates}
gives $F=\operatorname{id}$.
head: environment

label: ex:upperinterval
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:upperinterval}
For $a<b$, the upper interval $([a,b],u)$ is $q$-rigid.
If $x\le y$, it satisfies the chain from $a$ to $b$; if $x>y$,
the chain from $b$ to $a$ has all distances zero. Also $(a,b)$ is
the unique pair at directed distance $b-a$, so
Theorem~\ref{thm:diameter} applies.
head: environment

label: prop:maxcounter
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:maxcounter}
Plasticity of $(X,d^s)$ does not imply $q$-plasticity of $(X,d)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
On $\mathbb Z$ put $a_m=1+(1+2^m)^{-1}$ and
\[
d(m,n)=\begin{cases}0,&m=n,\\a_m,&m<n,\\2,&m>n.\end{cases}
\]
All nonzero distances lie in $(1,2]$. A triangle through a third distinct
point has right-hand side greater than $2$; repeated-point triangles are
immediate. Thus $d$ is a $T_0$-quasi-metric. Its symmetrization has constant
distance $2$ between distinct points, so every bijection is a metric isometry.
But $F(m)=m+1$ is bijective and $d$-nonexpansive: forward distances
strictly decrease and reverse distances stay $2$. It is not a $d$-isometry.
head: environment

title: Problem
body_md:
Find intrinsic conditions under which $e(X)$ is invariant under every
bijective nonexpansive self-map of $Q(X)$. In particular, characterize
canonical minimal pairs intrinsically and find recognition criteria for
noncompact hulls. Which spaces have $q$-plastic or $q$-rigid hulls?
head: environment

title: Problem
body_md:
Determine natural bicomplete asymmetric normed spaces that are q-LCDH.
For separable c-crowded quasi-metric spaces, which cardinalities and
descriptive complexities can be prescribed for dense $q$-rigid subspaces?
When can they be Borel, analytic or $\sigma$-compact?
head: environment

title: Problem
body_md:
Identify geometric conditions under which $q$-plasticity of $(X,d)$ is
equivalent to plasticity of $(X,d^s)$, or under which preservation of
$d^s$ by a bijective $d$-nonexpansive map forces preservation of $d$.
head: environment

title: Problem
body_md:
When does a separable asymmetric normed space contain a dense additive
subgroup $H$ on which every bijective $d_p$-nonexpansive map is an
isometry? When must every such map fixing $0$ be the identity, equivalently,
every such map be a translation?
head: environment

title: Problem
body_md:
Characterize two-sided directed intervals whose endpoints are preserved
by every bijective nonexpansive self-map without assuming a unique ordered
diametral pair. For hulls, find conditions making a bijective nonexpansive
map uniquely determined by its restriction to the canonical copy.
head: environment
